Sample 2 · Excel

An Excel reporting pack that ties.

Budget versus actual with variance in both pounds and per cent, in-cell data bars, a status column that says what it means rather than relying on a colour, and a totals row that adds up. Laid out so whoever picks it up next can follow it.

NW-Wholesale-Sales-Pack-Sep-2026.xlsx · Excel
Sample branch budget versus actual for September 2026.
A B C D E F
4 Branch Budget Actual Var £ Var % Status
5 Liverpool 88,000 93,000 +5,000 +5.7% On track
6 Manchester 98,000 105,000 +7,000 +7.1% Ahead of budget
7 Preston 54,000 50,000 −4,000 −7.4% Behind — review
8 Total 240,000 248,000 +8,000 +3.3%
Summary Branches Reconciliation Data

Variance both ways

Pounds and per cent. A −7.4% miss on a small branch and a −7.4% miss on a large one are very different problems.

Status in words

"Behind — review" is written out, not just shaded red, so the pack still works printed, photocopied, or for a colour-blind reader.

A totals row that ties

+5,000 +7,000 −4,000 = +8,000, and 8,000 / 240,000 = 3.3%. If the total doesn't reconcile, the report isn't finished.

Before & after

What automation actually changes.

The reporting output can look identical. What changes is who builds it, how long it takes, and whether you can trust it.

Before
  • Four exports pulled by hand every Monday
  • Copy-paste into a master workbook
  • Around three hours, every week
  • One person knows how it works
  • Nobody's certain the totals are right
After
  • Sources connected once, refreshed on a schedule
  • The report is waiting before anyone starts work
  • No manual steps to forget or get wrong
  • Documented, so it isn't in one person's head
  • Built-in reconciliation check on every refresh
3 hrs → 0

Other formats

Reports come in the shape that suits the job.

Not everything belongs in a dashboard. Part of the work is picking the right output for who's reading it.

Board and management packs

A fixed, point-in-time PDF or deck for a monthly meeting — consistent every month so figures are comparable across the year.

Scheduled email reports

The numbers land in the inbox of whoever needs them, at the time they need them, without anyone logging into anything.

Reconciliation reports

A standing check that two or more systems still agree — and a clear list of the records that don't, with the reason why.

Bank statement income reports

Raw statements turned into categorised income and outgoings — for affordability, lending, or a true picture of the money.

One-off deep dives

A single question answered properly: where did the margin go, which customers are really profitable, why did last quarter miss.

Excel model rebuilds

An inherited workbook nobody trusts, rebuilt so the formulas are auditable and the numbers can be defended.
